#4896. Viola Davis Says Shingles Pain Was a ‘9 Out of 10’: How It Changed Her Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony Award-winning actress and producer Viola Davis was 50 years old and at the height of her career when she developed shingles.

“All of a sudden, I got a rash in the middle of traveling and juggling [back-to-back] movies that started in the middle of my stomach [and] wrapped around my back,” she told Healthline. “And the pain was definitely at a 9 out of 10.”

Focused on work, Davis didn’t see a doctor right away. Her symptoms eventually subsided but later returned on her upper back.

“That is when I was like, ‘Oh, my goodness, I just got bitten by a poisonous spider,” said Davis. “It felt like really bad nerve pain…then someone mentioned the word shingles.”

After seeing a doctor, Davis learned she had shingles, which is caused by the same virus responsible for chickenpox. She also learned that the risk increases with age as the immune system naturally weakens.

“It can also lead to herpetic neuralgia, lifelong pain that can result from a shingles outbreak,” Robyn Liu, MD, member of the board of directors at the American Academy of Family Physicians, told Healthline.

Shingles can affect daily life, including work and sleep.

“Many people don’t realize that shingles can be associated with nerve pain, and for some, that pain can last for months or even years after the rash has resolved due to potential long-term complications,” Jennifer Caudle, DO, family medicine physician and associate professor at Rowan University School of Osteopathic Medicine, told Healthline.

Nearly one in three people in the U.S. develops shingles in their lifetime.

“Anyone who has had chickenpox can get it, but the risk goes up as we age,” said Liu.

After learning about shingles, Davis said she realized that she could no longer ignore her body.

“You just cannot. I mean, I know that people say it at nauseam, but, for me, it meant slowing down,” she said. “But then the shingles slowed me down…even though I was getting up, I was working out, [the] pain and the sluggishness was awful.”

Now 61, Davis has teamed up with GSK for its “Shingles, actually” campaign to raise awareness about shingles.

“[I’m] sending the message out there for women to really honor themselves and honor their bodies,” she said. “Their bodies literally speak. They’re the other character in their lives.”

After her experience with shingles, Davis began scheduling regular annual checkups.

“Before that time, I did absolutely go to my doctor, but only when it was absolutely necessary, you know, to get my colonoscopy, get my mammogram, but I never went if something felt odd,” said Davis.

Now, whenever she feels off, she doesn’t hesitate to see her doctor. She makes it a point to be honest with them about what’s going on with her body, and she is not shy about asking questions.

“I feel that it’s my job. It’s what I owe myself, and not only [do] I owe myself, it’s what I owe my daughter, it’s what I owe my husband, it’s what I owe my elderly mom, who is in advanced dementia [and] I take care of her,” Davis said.

Caudle stressed the importance of bringing questions to your doctor.

“That’s what we’re here for. Sometimes patients ​tell me they don’t realize they can ask questions or introduce a topic that their healthcare provider didn’t bring up first,” she said. “But a simple question like, ‘Am I at risk for shingles?’ can be a great place to begin.”

Davis has made stress reduction a priority. When she developed shingles, she was juggling an intense workload and adjusting to life as a new mom after adopting her daughter.

“I was someone who just ignored stress,” said Davis. “[When] we meet each other, it becomes a contest: Who can work through their stress the best? I felt like I had to strike while the iron was hot.”

Today, Davis makes stress reduction a priority through activities such as spraying her pillows with lavender, taking Epsom salt baths, meditating, going to therapy, exercising, spending time outdoors, using vagus nerve stimulation, and connecting with family and friends.

“It’s like I overdo it now because I feel like I have to overdo it in order to compete with my schedule. But that’s what I owe myself,” Davis said.

Still, her profession can be intense and time consuming due to shooting and promotional schedules. She still makes time to de-stress and focuses on projects that bring her joy.

“Your career is only as important as how much you enjoy it; how much it adds to your life,” said Davis. “[For] me, it used to be something that I felt defined my worth. I don’t feel like it defines my worth now…I feel that I’m already worthy… I was born worthy. That’s how I see it.”

Vaccination is the best way to protect against shingles, Liu said. The shingles vaccine is more than 90% effective at preventing the disease.

“For children, that protection begins with the chickenpox vaccine, which can be given along with other routine childhood immunizations. Preventing chickenpox also lowers the risk of developing shingles later in life,” she said.

Liu recommends two doses of the shingles vaccine for adults 50 and older, as well as adults 19 and older with weakened immune systems.

“Some patients may have more questions because side effects can be more noticeable than with other vaccines, so it’s important to understand the tradeoff: short-term discomfort from the vaccine versus the risk of lasting complications from shingles,” said Liu.

Side effects may include headache or redness, swelling, itching, and soreness where the shot was given.

“I tell my patients that these reactions are common and usually clear up within a day or two. They’re a normal sign that your body is building protection,” said Liu.

Most of a line designed for a million robots a year is installed, but he said it will take at least a year, possibly longer, to reach that rate of about 20,000 units a week, because parts of the design are still changing.

He listed what has to be solved first: the AI, the electromechanical design, and reliability, including making sure the robot doesn’t wear out after a month of use. He expects those issues to be solved around the end of next year. That’s when Tesla expects to deliver Optimus to companies outside Tesla, starting with industrial jobs that are dangerous, repetitive or need to run around the clock.

When an analyst asked where the design was still changing, a Tesla Optimus engineer pointed to the hand as one of the hardest hardware areas, along with custom gears that still carry reliability concerns. Musk agreed the hand is the main issue, explaining that fingers need to be soft enough to handle delicate objects while surviving constant wear, and robots can’t heal like human skin can.

On the AI side, Musk said Tesla is still working through problems with the AI architecture. Tesla doesn’t have a fleet of robots collecting data the way its cars do for FSD, so it plans to build 10,000 to 20,000 robots and have them practice tasks in what it calls an Optimus Academy. Tesla also plans to put its AI5 chip in Optimus around April 2027.

Musk also promised an Optimus video within a month or two showing the robot doing tasks that aren’t pre-programmed. He argued that many humanoid demos look impressive but only run scripted routines that wouldn’t hold up in the real world.

None of this is new. Last month, we reported that Tesla had ramped Optimus to hundreds of units a week, but that the robots couldn’t generalize to new tasks. According to The Information, the hand and forearm had over 100 small parts assembled by hand, touch sensors had reliability issues, and the AI could take days to learn basic tasks.

Tesla’s own Q3 shareholder letter now calls the bots coming off the Fremont line “the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured.” So every Optimus before this quarter wasn’t production quality.

And the timeline keeps moving. In 2024, Musk said Tesla would build Optimus for internal use in 2025 and hopefully in high volume for other companies in 2026. In January 2025, he said Tesla would build about 10,000 robots that year, with “several thousand” doing useful work by year-end. He later admitted none were. Now external deliveries are a late-2027 target.

Musk said on the call that, to the best of his knowledge, “there is no one that is even close to Tesla” on a general-purpose humanoid robot. That’s hard to square with what competitors have shown.

XPeng turned on an automated IRON production line in Guangzhou in September, with more than 80% of core processes automated. IRON has 21 degrees of freedom in each hand and runs XPeng’s physical AI model on three in-house Turing chips. XPeng plans mass production by the end of 2026, deliveries in the first half of 2027 starting with stores and malls, and a European rollout in the second half of 2027. That’s a similar timeline to Tesla’s, if not slightly ahead.

XPeng is dealing with the same reality. It hasn’t shipped IRON to a paying customer, and its timelines have slipped like everyone else’s.

Boston Dynamics started producing its electric Atlas in January and says all of its 2026 Atlas deployments are already committed, including to Google DeepMind, whose AI models Boston Dynamics is integrating. In September, it opened a robot training center at Hyundai’s Metaplant in Georgia, where Atlas is learning to sequence car parts for the assembly line. Hyundai plans to deploy 25,000 robots across its plants over the next few years. Boston Dynamics also hired Milan Kovac, Tesla’s former head of Optimus, in January.

Boston Dynamics also seems to have taken a more pragmatic approach to hands, prioritizing sturdy grippers for industrial parts over human-like dexterity. That’s less impressive in a demo, but it’s a way around the problem Tesla says is holding it back.

My prediction is that Optimus will forever be delayed. It's like FSD in Tesla cars -- never quite good enough to really take off and always one or two releases away from fixing everything. At least a Tesla car with a broken FSD is still a good car. Optimus with a bad brain is an interesting-looking boat anchor.

Tesla is facing the exact same problems as everyone else: hands that survive real work, robots reliable enough to pay for themselves, and AI that can handle tasks it wasn’t trained for. Nobody has cracked generalization yet, Tesla included. The difference is that Tesla’s competitors aren’t telling investors they have no competition.

Based on what’s public, XPeng has a more automated production line and a similar delivery date, and Boston Dynamics is already deploying Atlas in a car factory with committed customers. Tesla may well have the most robots built, but building robots isn’t the hard part. Making them useful is.

Tesla has promised a video in a month or two. If it shows Optimus doing real, unscripted work, great. But we’ve heard about Optimus timelines before, and they’ve slipped every year. Why should late 2027 be different?

#4893. A Famous Case of Shared Eyewitness 'Memory'

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

In previous posts of the Forensic View, we have seen that eyewitness memory, while frequently convincing to jurors and the public, is frequently and sometimes fabulously unreliable. But what happens when our confidence in reported eyewitness information is essentially “wired in parallel,” shared among different people who may, with repetition, put their own stamps on the information?

In 1914, during the First World War, these processes resulted in strongly held beliefs that Russian troops were coming.

All histories of that terrible conflict discuss the importance of Russian military operations in Eastern Europe. The hardships and horrifying casualty counts of that very harsh campaign are well attested.

But none of that happened in Scotland, where tens of thousands of entirely imaginary Russians were firmly believed to have turned up anyway.

The whole mess seems to have started on August 27th, 1914, when there was a long delay in the railway service linking London and Liverpool. Somebody, perhaps in an ill-advised attempt to boost morale, explained to somebody else that this was due to the diversion of trains which were transporting thousands of Russian troops, who had landed in Scotland, to reinforce the Western Front.

Word spread. These Russians’ route was allegedly very specific; they had crossed the Arctic Sea to Norway, then traveled by steamship to Aberdeen, and from there were being carried by special troop trains to the Channel ports.

Now, prior frameworks for understanding strongly influence our ability to remember and interpret information (Bransford & Johnson, 1973), even when those frameworks are completely incorrect, and the resulting memories and interpretations are therefore complete rubbish (Sharps, 2024; Sharps & Price-Sharps, 2026). However, when such frameworks, accurate or not, are filled with plausible feature-intensive detail, people may be increasingly inclined to believe them (Sharps, 2022, 2024); and the specificity of these peripatetic Russians’ itineraries helped to convince people of their absolute reality.

Additional details followed. Witnesses had supposedly seen Russians stamping snow off their boots at railway stations (Pennell, 2015). Makes sense—Russia has a lot of snow. Granted, how those troops managed to maintain that snow on their boots all the way to Edinburgh in August is quite a mystery (Tuchman, 1962); but since the story included the very specific detail of an imaginary railway porter who had swept up the imaginary snow, who was going to argue with this imaginary account?

Very reliable people had supposedly seen these Russians. An Oxford professor knew a colleague who’d been summoned as a Russian translator, and a Scots army officer had seen their big fur caps and, believe it or not, their bows and arrows. Why these Russian troops lacked modern weapons remains unexplained, but with enough popular momentum behind the story, people believed it anyway. The people of the time were under the extraordinary stress of horrible new types of warfare that produced casualty rates virtually beyond comprehension for that day—and it has been shown that when people are under stress, they are more likely to ignore evidentiary flaws in accounts (Sharps et al., 2013; Sharps, 2024).

Evidently, this psychological effect extended to snow in August and 20th-century Russian infantrymen armed like Robin Hood.

A Scots landowner personally reported 125,000 Russians marching across his property (Tuchman, 1962), which seems a bit low when 500,000 imaginary Russians were originally reported; but gradually these imaginary numbers dropped down to an equally imaginary 70,000 or 80,000, which presumably made people feel more confident about the realism of the whole imaginary business.

Some actual history became involved in this mess, as well. The naval battle of Heligoland Bight, which had nothing whatsoever to do with Russians, was explained as some form of weird diversion to cover the sea transport of these imaginary forces to Belgium (Tuchman, 1962). On the continent, people waited en masse in Paris to welcome their Cossack defenders. The Germans became concerned as well (Tuchman, 1962). Contemporary reports held that the Kaiser and his senior staff had left France from fear of the “250,000” Russian troops believed to be in the field there, and the German Army was reported to have detached two sorely needed divisions to repel this imaginary invasion from the Steppes.

Readers today may find this account mildly amusing, but essentially irrelevant to our modern lives. The First World War seems lost in remote antiquity, with the Red Baron, perhaps better known today for pizza than for aerial victories, flying about in a powered box-kite, and antique cannons being dragged around mud-soaked battlefields by teams of panicked horses. The whole thing may seem as remote to modern people as Crecy or Agincourt.

But if you were able to examine the brain of a person in 1914, you would find no substantive difference between that brain and the one in the head of any modern Internet-ridden person today. The effects of inaccurate prior frameworks, of stress-related reduction in critical thinking, and of the uncritical sharing of purported eyewitness accounts would be psychologically the same in the worlds of 1914 and 2026.

However, there would be an important exception today, based on our technology rather than our psychology. Unlike the word-of-mouth campaigns that spread false rumors in clubs and at railway stations in 1914, we of 2026 have the internet to spread false rumors worldwide at electronic speeds, either by mistake or by design on the part of people who have something to gain. We also have AI-generated imagery so advanced that its products are virtually impossible for most of us to tell from reality.

The remote and imaginary reports of Russians in Scotland in 1914 are more than a quaint episode in the history of eyewitness memory. They form a significant warning for those of us in the modern age of technology. Today, more than in any previous era, we must be very careful in our assessment of evidence, eyewitness, visual, and otherwise, and very aware of how the principles governing our psychology may influence that assessment.

Bransford, J. D., and Johnson, M. K. 1973. Considerations of Some Problems of Comprehension. In W. G. Chase (Ed.), Visual Information Processing. Orlando, FL: Academic Press.

Pennell, C. 2015. Believing the Unbelievable: The Myth of the Russians with 'Snow On Their Boots' in the United Kingdom, 1914. Cultural and Social History, 11, 69-87.

Sharps, M.J. 2022. Processing Under Pressure: Stress, Memory, and Decision-Making in Law Enforcement (3rd ed.). Park City, Utah: Blue 360 Media.

Sharps, M.J. 2024. The Forensic View: Investigative Psychology, Law Enforcement, Space Aliens, Exploration, and the Nature of Madness. Las Vegas: Amazon.

Sharps, M.J., Herrera, M.R., and Price‐Sharps, J.L. 2013. Situationally Equivocal Eyewitness Evidence and the Violence of Crimes. Journal of Investigative Psychology and Offender Profiling, 10, DOI: 10.1002/jip.1398

Sharps, M.J., & Price-Sharps, J.L. 2026. Dissociation and Belief: The Psychology of Why Things Go Horribly Wrong, and What To Do About It. Las Vegas: Amazon.

Tuchman, B.W. 1962. The Guns of August. New York: Ballantine.

#4892. Bijan Robinson Has a Secret Weapon. It’s Not What You Think.

The Falcons star approaches this area of health with the same discipline as his game.

BIJAN ROBINSON DOESN’T lack confidence. The Atlanta Falcons running back has been one of the best players at his position even before his days in the NFL, when he was a top back at the University of Texas and a number one-rated recruit going into college. He’s not afraid to show it, either. “If you know me, [you know] I smile a lot,” he tells Men’s Health.

As much as he has depended on his smile to project his self-assurance, Robinson didn’t always feel the best about his teeth. He recalls some slightly awkward stages in his younger years. “When I was a kid, more middle school, I was still kind of growing into my teeth,” he says. “I had two teeth that would kind of twist in a little bit.”

For lots of guys, the state of their smile is a huge concern. But Robinson didn’t want to go through the trouble of getting braces to address the issue. “I was still trying to avoid having a wire on my teeth, because I thought that it would limit me from eating certain things, trying to keep it straight.” Robinson grew into his smile, and didn’t worry as much about his teeth as he became one of the most celebrated football players in the country.

But when he eventually entered the NFL, he realized how a small fix could make a big difference for his professional image. Robinson partnered with Invisalign and began wearing the clear aligners to straighten out that little twist in his smile.

“You're in front of a camera a lot in interviews and even just talking to people [at] events,” he says. “Having [my] smile is not only a confidence booster for myself, but the other I'm talking to—it makes them more engaged in the conversation. They see you take care of yourself.”

Robinson says he wears the aligners everywhere—even with his helmet on in practice and in games. He says a traditional mouthguard makes it difficult for him to breathe, and his conditioning is what gives him an edge as a back who can score out of the backfield as a runner and receiver. (Invisalign reps clarified it should not be used as a mouthguard).

Overall, Robinson appreciates how he’s able to make his oral health another aspect of the self-discipline and self-improvement practices that have helped him to be such a standout player. Like his workouts and skill-position drills, he takes it seriously. His smile is also his responsibility. “I'm not only representing myself,” he says. “I'm representing the Falcons, my family—everybody.”

Brett Williams, NASM-CPT, PES, a senior editor at Men's Health, is a certified trainer and former pro football player and tech reporter. You can find his work elsewhere at Mashable, Thrillist, and other outlets.

#4890. PMOS, Formerly PCOS, May Be Associated with Alzheimer's Disease Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), formerly known as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), has been linked to changes in brain function and cognition that may overlap with those seen in Alzheimer’s disease.

However, a review published October 13 in the Journal of the Endocrine Society suggests that metabolic conditions commonly associated with PMOS, rather than PMOS itself, may help explain a potential link to Alzheimer’s disease and dementia risk.

“Researchers are exploring whether some metabolic conditions commonly seen in women with PMOS, such as insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes, [and] elevated cholesterol, could play a role in dementia, since these are already known risk factors for cognitive decline,” Yesika Garcia, MD, board certified endocrinologist with Medical Offices of Manhattan, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline.

“In other words, any potential connection may be related to these underlying metabolic issues rather than PMOS itself. I think it’s important to clarify that an association does not mean causation,” she added.

The researchers searched PubMed for studies published through 2025 examining brain structure and function, cognitive performance, biomarkers associated with neurodegenerative diseases, and dementia risk in people with PMOS.

Because PMOS is a newer term, the researchers searched for studies using both PMOS and PCOS.

The review identified studies suggesting that people with PMOS may experience mild differences in certain cognitive abilities, including:

Some brain imaging studies using MRI and PET scans identified differences in brain structure and function among people with PMOS. Researchers also observed hormonal changes associated with differences in gray matter.

Some studies identified elevated biomarkers associated with Alzheimer’s disease in people with PMOS. These findings appeared to overlap with metabolic changes seen in type 2 diabetes, particularly those associated with obesity and insulin resistance.

The researchers also found that neurological differences were less pronounced when people with PMOS were compared with metabolically healthy control groups, suggesting that associated metabolic conditions may play an important role in these findings.

Overall, the review suggests that metabolic conditions associated with PMOS may contribute to changes in brain health, although more research is needed to determine whether PMOS independently affects Alzheimer’s disease or dementia risk.

“I think we need to be careful about drawing conclusions too early. The research raises some good questions, but it doesn’t prove that PCOS [PMOS] causes Alzheimer’s disease,” said Dung Trinh, MD, internist, of MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“What it does reinforce is how important metabolic health may be when it comes to protecting our brains as we get older,” he added.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the study, agreed. She also added that more attention and research need to be given to PMOS, brain changes, and future risks of dementia.

There are various ways that PMOS and dementia may share pathways and overlap, according to the researchers. Some of these shared pathways include:

Trinh explained that insulin resistance may be one of the most important connections between PMOS and dementia.

Although insulin is commonly associated with diabetes and blood sugar regulation, it also plays an important role in brain function. When insulin signaling doesn’t work properly, it may interfere with how brain cells use energy, potentially contributing to problems with memory and thinking over time.

Chronic inflammation, which can occur in people with PMOS, may also play a role in Alzheimer’s disease, Trinh told Healthline.

“Researchers are looking at how these metabolic changes may affect amyloid and tau, two proteins associated with Alzheimer’s. Some brain imaging studies have even found differences in brain structure and function among women with PCOS [PMOS],” he said.

Ross added that elevated androgen levels, which are common in people with PMOS, may also play a role in dementia risk.

“An important distinction is that these risk factors are not present in every woman with PMOS, and having PMOS does not automatically mean someone will experience cognitive decline,” cautioned Garcia.

Garcia noted that many of the dementia risk factors associated with PMOS are modifiable.

“Regular exercise, including both cardiovascular activity and strength training, can improve insulin sensitivity, help with weight management, and support cardiovascular and brain health,” she added.

“A Mediterranean-style diet, with plenty of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, healthy fats, and lean sources of protein, is a reasonable place to start,” he said.

Managing blood sugar, cholesterol, and blood pressure is also important, Trinh and Garcia noted.

“Medication, like metformin, can also improve insulin resistance, which may further reduce the risk of dementia,” Ross added.

Getting adequate sleep, avoiding smoking, and staying mentally and socially active are additional ways to support long-term brain health, Garcia told Healthline.

“For someone with PCOS [PMOS], I would encourage regular visits with their healthcare provider to monitor metabolic health and address problems early,” said Trinh.

“While we cannot say that these interventions specifically prevent dementia in women with PMOS, we know they benefit overall metabolic and cardiovascular health, which are closely connected to brain health,” explained Garcia.

#4889. Why We Delay Important Decisions

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

I’m sure you can relate to putting off an important decision until next week, then the week after that, and then the week after that. Maybe you need to decide where you would like to relocate, choose a healthcare provider, or determine whether to move forward with an important medical procedure. You know the decision needs your attention, but you keep finding reasons to wait.

Most of us may think of procrastination as putting things off because we are busy or lack motivation. However, what if we are not avoiding the task itself, but the uncertainty that comes with making a decision? Oftentimes, the most difficult part is not knowing what to do, but accepting that we cannot predict how things will turn out.

Experts argue that one reason this happens is negative reinforcement. When avoiding something uncomfortable brings relief, our brains will likely desire to avoid it again. Consider, for example, when a deadline gets pushed back. In the moment, you may feel better knowing you have more time to complete the task at hand, even though you know that the work still needs to get done. Delaying an important decision can have the same effect. We may receive temporary relief, however the decision still remains unresolved.

In my work with people facing difficult life decisions, I have seen how the desire to avoid making the wrong choice can become a significant barrier. People may spend considerable time weighing possibilities, seeking reassurance, and revisiting the same concerns.

Another reason important decisions can be difficult to make is that we want to make the best possible choice. Experts describe this tendency as maximizing. It involves searching for the best available option, rather than choosing one that meets our needs and priorities. Wanting to make a good decision is reasonable, but constantly searching for something better can make it harder to settle on an option.

Let's think about someone deciding whether to relocate for a new job. The opportunity they are considering may offer better pay and career growth, however accepting it could mean leaving family, familiar surroundings, and comfort. They may continue comparing options and questioning whether another opportunity would have been better, even after obtaining enough information to inform their decision.

Recent research offers some insight into this pattern. For instance, in a 2024 study, researchers examined how people with maximizing tendencies estimate the time they spend making decisions. Results showed that "maximizers" tended to underestimate how much time they spent comparing and reconsidering their options. They likely don't realize they are making decision-making harder not easier for themselves.

Making a decision becomes even more challenging when we are faced with too many options to select from. For instance, someone who has decided to undergo a medical procedure, but must choose how to pay for it, has to decide on using a credit card, applying for a medical credit line, choosing an in-house payment plan, or financing through a third-party company, which adds another decision to an already important one.

One emerging example in the healthcare industry is "first-look financing." An article by Cherry describes how this concept introduces one preferred financing option first while keeping other options available. This approach reflects choice architecture, which examines how the presentation of choices can influence people's decisions.

For example, after a patient agrees to move forward with a medical procedure, the clinic might first explain its preferred third-party financing option, including the monthly payment and application process. If the patient is not comfortable with that option, the provider can then discuss other options, such as an in-house payment plan or using a credit card.

Here are a few ways to make important decisions feel more manageable:

Putting off important decisions is something many of us experience, especially when we are uncertain about what may happen next. Avoiding a decision can make us feel better temporarily, but it does not necessarily make the situation easier. Ultimately, we do not have to find the perfect option or know exactly how everything will turn out before moving forward. Sometimes, making a good-enough decision and taking one small step at a time is what can help us move past the uncertainty.

Cheek, N. N., & Schwartz, B. (2016). On the meaning and measurement of maximization. Judgment and Decision Making, 11(2), 126–146. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1930297500007257

Huang and Li (2024). “How Maximizers Estimate Their Decision Time: The Mediating Effect of Memory Reduction.” Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 37(3).

#4888. Scania speeds up switch to silent semi trucks with Chinese production

Record fuel prices driven by the dumb oil war in Iran are fueling a faster-than-expected switch to electric trucks in the world’s biggest freight markets – and Swedish heavy truck brand Scania is scrambling to meet demand with a new factory in China.

The Swedish truck maker is set to begin manufacturing battery-powered trucks at its new Rugao assembly plant in China as soon as it receives a license, according to Scania Chief Executive Officer Christian Levin.

In an interview given in Södertälje, Levin said he expects electric trucks to account for half of China’s market by the start of 2027. “We have had to speed up those plans,” Levin explained. “It’s always quite a complicated process in China to get licenses to do different things, but I have to say: it has moved much faster than we could have imagined.”

Chinese electric semi truck sales jumped almost 80% in the first half of 2026 compared to 2025, and are on pace to account for over 30% of all heavy trucks sold this year – and that pace is accelerating.

Scania built the Rugao plant last year, making it the Traton Group’s first wholly-owned factory in China. The facility will serve China and other Asian markets, and can build both conventional diesel and battery-powered trucks on the same assembly lines.

“It is happening quickly and that’s incredibly fascinating,” says Levin. “It means they have found a way to expand charging infrastructure and the power grid, which is the biggest challenge we have in many countries around the world, including Europe.”

#4887. RJ Mitte's Death Highlights Mental Health Challenges for People With Cerebral Palsy

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Breaking Bad” actor and disability advocate RJ Mitte has died at age 34.

Mitte reportedly died by suicide, his representative told People on October 12. However, local authorities have said the official cause and manner of his death remain under investigation.

Mitte, who was best-known for playing Walter White Jr. on the Emmy Award-winning television series “Breaking Bad,” lived with cerebral palsy and advocated for disability inclusion.

There is currently no evidence to suggest that cerebral palsy caused the actor’s death. Still, Mitte’s untimely passing highlights the mental health challenges that people with cerebral palsy may face.

Research has demonstrated elevated risks of anxiety and depression among those with the condition, alongside barriers to diagnosis, social participation, and employment.

“Living with cerebral palsy can affect mental health through several interacting pathways,” said Shannel Elhelou, neuropsychologist and founder of Brain Centric Neuropsychology in Westlake Village, CA.

“Chronic pain, fatigue, disrupted sleep, and the effort required to navigate daily activities can take an emotional toll. Experiences of bullying, discrimination, social exclusion, and difficulty accessing care can add to that burden. Also, the early brain injury underlying cerebral palsy may contribute to difficulties with emotional regulation, although each person’s experience is different,” Elhelou told Healthline.

If you or someone you know is in crisis and considering suicide or self-harm, please seek support:

If you’re calling on behalf of someone else, stay with them until help arrives. You may remove weapons or substances that can cause harm if you can do so safely.

If you’re not in the same household, stay on the phone with them until help arrives.

Mitte played a key role in challenging stereotypes by portraying a teenager with cerebral palsy on “Breaking Bad.”

Outside of acting, Mitte advocated for people with disabilities through organizations including United Cerebral Palsy (UCP) and Shriners Children’s.

He also led the Mitte Foundation, a non-profit corporation founded in 1994 by his grandparents, Roy F. and Joann Cole Mitte, that improves the quality of life for people in Central Texas.

Mitte’s advocacy emphasized representation, inclusion, and opportunities for people with disabilities.

The legacy he leaves behind underscores the need to recognize mental health as an essential part of care for individuals with cerebral palsy and other disabilities.

Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of conditions affecting movement, posture, and coordination.

Most people with cerebral palsy have typical intelligence, although some also have intellectual disabilities or other comorbid physical and mental health conditions.

A 2018 study published in JAMA Neurology found that adults with cerebral palsy had a 28% higher risk of developing depression and a 40% higher risk of anxiety than adults without the condition.

A 2024 study in JAMA Network Open found higher recorded rates of anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) among children and young adults with cerebral palsy.

The researchers also identified comparatively low rates of depression and suicidal ideation, highlighting concerns that these conditions may be underdiagnosed.

“Research shows that adults with cerebral palsy have an increased risk of depression and anxiety,” Elhelou said.

“However, these conditions should never be viewed as an inevitable part of having a disability. One concern is ‘diagnostic overshadowing,’ when symptoms of depression, anxiety, or other mental health conditions are attributed to cerebral palsy itself, leading those conditions to go unrecognized and untreated. Someone’s fatigue, withdrawal, or changes in behavior deserve careful assessment rather than the assumption that ‘this is just their cerebral palsy,'” she continued.

“While these findings help us understand mental health risks among people with cerebral palsy, they cannot tell us what any one person was experiencing. Many interacting factors may contribute to someone dying by suicide, and it would be inappropriate to attribute an individual’s death to their disability.”

A 2019 study published in Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology found that children with cerebral palsy had higher odds of anxiety disorders and behavioral challenges than children without the condition.

Difficulties with friendships and bullying were associated with some of these differences.

Factors that may affect well-being include:

The researchers also found that supportive friendships may help reduce some of these disparities, reinforcing the importance of inclusive schools and communities.

A 2021 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that U.S. adults with disabilities faced increased risks of suicidal thoughts, planning, and attempts compared with adults without disabilities.

The 988 Lifeline received more than 8 million contacts through calls, texts, chats, and American Sign Language videophone in 2025, according to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration.

Federal funding for the Lifeline’s dedicated LGBTQ+ youth service ended in July 2025, removing the option to press 3 for specialized support.

After pressure from Congress, the service was recently restored at the end of September, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation (KFF).

Employment and financial independence can influence well-being for anyone, particularly those with cerebral palsy.

However, a 2024 study found that just 30.4% of young adults with cerebral palsy who participated in vocational rehabilitation programs were employed when they exited those programs.

Workplace accommodations, accessible hiring, vocational rehabilitation, and inclusive social opportunities can help address these barriers.

“Depression and anxiety are treatable, and they should never be dismissed as an inevitable part of living with a disability,” Elhelou said.

“If you notice persistent sadness, anxiety, hopelessness, or withdrawal, reach out to someone you trust and a mental health professional. You deserve a clinician who takes your concerns seriously and adapts treatment to your communication, mobility, or other access needs. Care should also address pain, fatigue, and sleep difficulties, which can affect emotional well-being.”

Organizations such as United Cerebral Palsy offer information and support for people with cerebral palsy and their families.

Healthcare professionals can also improve outcomes by screening for mental health concerns, using appropriate assessment tools, and connecting patients with accessible treatment.

Improved access to care, inclusive communities, and meaningful opportunities can help people with cerebral palsy and other disabilities thrive.

“Asking for help does not diminish your resilience or your contributions. If you are experiencing thoughts of suicide or feel overwhelmed, you do not have to wait until things feel unbearable to reach out,” Elhelou said.

“Supportive relationships, peer groups, and disability communities can offer connection and understanding. Staying engaged in activities that bring enjoyment and meaning can also help.”

#4885. The Men's Health Ultimate Guide to Peptides

A science-backed guide to understanding the use, side effects, and supporting research behind the emerging substances.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

AS THE CURIOSITY around peptides grows, the FDA has made efforts in removing a portion of the 19 synthetic peptides from the Category 2 Bulk Substances List. This is kind of a huge deal because when the FDA classifies a substance as Category 2 they believe that it carries significant safety risks, and prohibit compounding pharmacies from making it.

In July 2026, an FDA advisory committee met to evaluate evidence for seven popular synthetic peptides on the Category 2 list and recommend whether the FDA should move them onto the Category 1 list, which allows them to be made. Another five will be under review in 2027.The FDA is not bound to the advisory committee’s recommendations.

The panel voted to loosen the restrictions on BPC-157 and TB-500 (those make up the infamous “Wolverine Stack”), as well as KPV, MOTS-C, Epitalon and Semax. It voted no for Emedeltide; that’s the one people reach for to help their sleep. None of the compounds scored a unanimous vote. This October, US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. pushed forward a policy to temporarily increase access to these six unapproved peptides. The government will not penalize licensed pharmacists in compounding pharmacies for creating and distributing these substances for people with a prescription. The nudge from RFK Jr. to allow the temporary sale of peptides has received mixed reactions.

”The American Peptide Association applauds the efforts of the Trump Administration and HHS to green light certain peptides into production by compound pharmacies,” Jeff Cohen, cofounder of the American Peptide Association wrote in an email to MH. “It is much needed clarity that the peptide industry, clinicians and consumers have hoped and worked for for the past couple years and is a bold step outside the usual pharma driven, FDA managed pathway.”

Motisola Lewis, MD, is an internal medicine physician who runs her own concierge medical practice working to fix a broken medical system. While she focuses on providing personalized care to her patients, she doesn’t agree with expanding access to unapproved peptides before having adequate evidence of their safety and effectiveness. “I want patients to have access to promising treatments, but I also want those treatments to be supported by good science. My concern is that the enthusiasm around peptides has moved much faster than the clinical evidence.” For Dr. Lewis, several questions are still missing that the FDA has not answered: do these peptides actually work and for whom, peptide quality especially from third-party suppliers, and who is in charge of oversight. That doesn’t mean she is unwilling to discuss peptides, which is happening more than ever.

Sritha Rajupet, MD, MPH, chair of the department of family, population, and preventive medicine at Stony Brook Medicine, also has concerns. “Most of these peptides still lack high-quality human data on safety, effectiveness, and appropriate dosing,” Dr. Rajupet says. Meaning that even if the FDA removes the Category 2 label, there’s still not a lot of research around if and how they work—along with any side effects. In the document outlining RFK Jr’s new policy, compounding pharmacists must report “serious adverse events, and product quality issues to FDA and to the States where the products are compounded.”

Still, Dr. Rajupet acknowledges that people are interested in synthetic peptides—and many are already obtaining them through unregulated channels.

Kent Bradley, MD, sees this at his role of chief medical officer at 10X Health, which offers synthetic peptide therapy. “Many of the people reaching for peptides have already exhausted conventional options,” he says. “The issue we are seeing is that individuals may have gotten a peptide without going through legitimate quality checks of a compounded pharmacy and self-administering based on information they are seeing off of social media.”

The world of synthetic peptides is promising, for sure. But there are dangers—some of which are serious (ahem, cancer). Dr. Rajupet says that in order for consumers to protect themselves, they have to study up.

“From a clinical perspective, the priority is balancing harm reduction with scientific rigor—engaging patients in open, nonjudgmental conversations while being clear that many of these therapies remain experimental, with uncertain risks and benefits,” says Dr. Rajupet.

For this reason, we created a one-stop glossary to help answer your questions about the current peptide-palooza we’re in now. Here’s the hype—and actual science.

WELL, KNOW THAT peptides exist naturally. Technically, they’re short chains of amino acids, the building blocks of protein. And not just the kind of protein that builds biceps. Proteins can also act as messengers throughout your body, doing everything from signaling the release a particular hormone to regulating inflammatory responses.

But when we’re talking about the kind of peptides the FDA will consider for deregulation, we’re talking about synthetic peptides delivered through sprays or injection. These drugs work to trigger the same responses as natural peptides, but the science is in its very early stages. Anecdotal evidence from who take peptides have reported improvements in their health, appearance, and muscle performance. But, again, anecdotal.

These are the synthetic peptides that the FDA will consider for deregulation in 2026 and 2027, broken into categories based on their supposed health benefits. And we gave each a thumbs up, thumbs down, or thumbs "meh" to rate just how much the science backs up the supposed benefits.

Known as the fat burning peptide, AOD-9604 mimics human growth hormone to promote lipolysis, or the breakdown of stored fat. Scientists are using the peptide as a possible treatment for obesity and people are taking the peptide recreationally to burn body fat, boost fat metabolism, and support body recomposition. There is also discussion of AOD-9604 helping with joint pain, mobility, and collagen production. One of the supposed benefits of AOD-9604 is that it sheds fat without affecting blood sugar or inducing insulin resistance.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: The studies on the effectiveness and safety of AOD-9604 go back roughly a decade. The research was largely conducted on animals and most of the studies that showed positive results were funded or led by researchers from the pharmaceutical company that developed AOD-9604.

This peptide reportedly protects the cell by providing more “fuel” for increased stamina. So people who report fatigue are taking the peptide to improve energy and metabolism. Because MOTS-C is supposed to target mitochondria, the energy sources of a cell, you’ll see it promoted in longevity stacks.RESEARCH SUMMARY: While there has been extensive research into the physiological function of MOTS-C, there is a lack of clinical trial data testing the safety and effectiveness of the peptide.

Semax is considered a brain-boosting peptide often given as a nasal spray. Anecdotal reports detail improvements in memory, attention, and deeper mental awareness. Semax is supposed to work by raising a protein called brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) that is important for learning and strengthening connection between brain cells.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Most of the research in Semax that claims it has neuroprotective effects come from Russia, where the peptide is used in the treatment of people with stroke. The Alzheimer’s Drug Discovery Foundation reviewed the Russian pilot studies in humans and found a lack of strong evidence demonstrating that Semax would improve cognition in healthy individuals or in the prevention of cognitive aging. (Although a recent 2025 study from Russia found evidence of Semax injections reducing amyloid plaques in rat models of Alzheimer’s). Older studies using rats found improved cognition 15 minutes after injection, likely by stimulating BDNF production. There is a lack of safety data, especially in long-term side effects, in humans. One review reported discoloration of the nasal cavity and increased blood sugar levels in people with diabetes. Not great.

Selank is a nootropic touted for reducing anxiety and stress while increasing cognitive performance. Anecdotal evidence calls Selank a “life-changer” for anxiety and sleep, with some people feeling relaxed but not drowsy, as well as more focused.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Selank’s anxiolytic and cognitive protective effect along with relieving stress have only been studied in rodents and molecular studies. Older mice studies have also found evidence of improved learning and memory performance after a single injection of Selank.

TB-500 is a peptide intended for muscle recovery, increased flexibility, and joint stability. Users often pair the synthetic peptide with BPC-157 to further boost muscle recovery. TB-500 works by binding to a structural protein in cells called actin. By up-regulating actin, TB-500 purportedly speeds cell movement for tissue repair.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: There is a good amount of animal research on Thymosin Beta-4 and its accelerated healing effects on skin and muscle fibers. While there is a body of preclinical research on the peptide, there’s a lack of studies looking at the synthetic peptide TB-500. Plus, there is no clinical evidence in humans that Thymosin Beta-4 or TB-500 repairs muscles or increases athletic performance.

More concerning are studies linking elevated Thymosin Beta-4 levels with the development of cancer. Through the same mechanisms that promote wound healing, Thymosin Beta-4 may enhance tumor angiogenesis, the process where cancer cells stimulate new blood vessels, which provides them oxygen and nutrients to grow and spread.

Known as the “Wolverine” or “Body Protection Compound,” the synthetic peptide reportedly helps with tissue repair and anti-inflammatory effects. Users champion the peptide’s ability to speed recovery from intensive workouts or even injury. BPC-157 does not directly build muscle mass.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Animal data on BPC-157 showed evidence of the peptide helping with musculoskeletal injuries. However, there is little data showing the effects in humans.

The natural form of this peptide helps with increasing and restoring immune function. It works by enhancing antibody response and T-cell activity. People taking the synthetic, injectable form report immediate improvement in their well-being after long COVID and other immune disorders. Outside of the US, Thymosin Alpha-1 is approved in over 30 countries for treating hepatitis and other infections.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Five large clinical trials on the peptide have found Thymosin Alpha-1 reduces inflammation and infection in people with severe acute pancreatitis. That’s likely due to the peptide’s ability to rebalance immune cell distribution, including boosting the percentages of CD4+ T cells. Thymosin Alpha-1 has also been shown to enhance vaccine response and help people with severe COVID by repairing damage caused by inflammation. However, one large phase 3 clinical trial in people with sepsis found an injection of thymosin alpha 1 did not improve mortality outcomes.

People taking the synthetic form of this peptide report doing so to reduce inflammation and improve skin health. (Some say it can clear up eczema, psoriasis, and acne.) There are also some people with inflammatory bowel conditions, such as Crohn’s and IBD, who say that KPV has helped their gut health. The peptide reportedly works by inhibiting several pro-inflammatory pathways while preserving other immune responses.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: There’s not sufficient data on KPV to conclusively say it helps in humans. The most cited research on KPV is a 2008 study, which found that the peptide reduced intestinal inflammation in human intestinal cells. Yes, that was many, many years ago.

This neuropeptide reportedly promotes falling asleep faster, as well as increasing how much time you spend in restorative deep, slow-wave sleep. in Stage 3 sleep. Anecdotal evidence of people taking the synthetic form of this peptide states that in helps with staying asleep, increasing sleep duration, and entering deep sleep.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: DSIP research on humans is extremely limited. Most research looking into DSIP’s role in sleep took place in the 1980s and 1990s—with mixed results. While a small clinical trial did report sleep-promoting effects, other studies found it ineffective or from a placebo effect. Research in the 2000s has been focused on animals and how DSIP could help protect against cancer or improve motor ability after stroke.

This peptide has links to sexual function. It works by stimulating the release of the hormone, gonadotropin, which results in an increase of testosterone. People who take synthetic kisspeptin-10 have reported a greater libido, ability to maintain an erection, and enjoy orgasm, along with reduced anxiety—especially surrounding sexual response.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: There is animal and human research that shows kisspeptin-10 stimulates gonadotrophin release. Most notably, a small clinical trial found that men with low sexual desire experienced increases in “penile tumescence” (their term, not ours), as well as greater attraction and arousal. There were no side effects reported.

Epitalon is the natural form of the peptide, and it’s been used to treat chronic insomnia, especially in people who don’t respond to sleep medications. By raising melatonin, the peptide would allegedly regulate circadian rhythms and promote better sleep. Epithalamin is the synthetic peptide and people are reportedly taking it for anti-aging effects, both cognitive and aesthetic.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Epitalon has not been tested in people for slowing or preventing cognitive decline. Most of the early preclinical and clinical studies on epitalon’s effects on anti-aging, cognition, and sleep come from Russia and mainly from the lab of the now-deceased Dr. Vladimir Kh. Khavinson. The few studies in human cells (note, not actual humans) suggest that epitalon extends telomere length. Telomeres are the protective caps at the end of chromosomes to protect from damage. In terms of safety, there is a lack of data, especially on its short-term and long-term toxicity effects.

The natural GHK-Cu peptide is used for promoting skin health. People using the synthetic drug are using GHK-Cu to stimulate collagen and elastin production to tighten aging skin, reduce wrinkles, fade scars, and repair the skin barrier. People have anecdotally reported thicker, fuller hair after using the peptide as it supposedly reduces inflammation and increases blood circulation to the scalp.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Topical GHK-Cu is commonly used in cosmetics to increase collagen production, promote wound healing, and improve skin health. It has a good safety profile because it has limited low-level skin absorption. Injectable and oral versions of GHK-Cu may come with several potentially life-threatening risks.

This peptide is a selective agonist of the ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHSR1) that stimulates the pituitary gland to release growth hormone production. (Yeah, it’s complex.) Just know that people are excited about Ipamorelin because the peptide reportedly increases muscle mass and strength.

Online forums dedicated to Ipamorelin mention that taking the peptide does not increase appetite, cortisol, or prolactin like other growth hormone peptides. In addition to strength improvements, other ancedotes discuss skin and hair benefits. Ipamorelin is typically paired with other peptides, such as CJC-1295.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Animal studies have shown that Ipamorelin is effective in stimulating the pituitary gland to release growth hormones. However, there is a lack of large clinical trials that show the peptide works in humans.

This peptide binds to receptors in the pituitary gland to stimulate the secretion of growth hormone and production of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1). People are taking CJC-1295 to build muscle, reduce recovery time, and increase fat metabolism. A common stack among the longevity community is CJC-1295 and Ipamorelin for its synergistic effects to maintain lean muscle, get better sleep, and reduce fatigue.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: While clinical data has shown promising results of CJC-1295 to increase growth hormone production, the peptide is linked to a number of adverse events.

The following five peptides are likely to stay on the Category 2 list because of a lack of clinical evidence and/or significant safety concerns.

SIDE EFFECTS: Infection, potential death, fluctuating blood sugar levels, pancreatitis

SIDE EFFECTS: Increase appetite, possible changes in cortisol levels, and increases in blood sugar levels

USE: “Sunless” tanning and to stimulate erections in men with erectile dysfunction

SIDE EFFECTS: Severe adverse events including melanoma, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, sympathomimetic toxidrome, and priapism

USE: Increasing immune defenses and fight against infections

SIDE EFFECTS: Nonclinical research has found adverse effects on the male reproduction system and potentially cancer development

SIDE EFFECTS: Insufficient information on whether it’s safe for humans

#4884. Pope Leo XIV Diagnosed With Lung Cancer After Surgery to Remove Part of Lung

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer following a successful surgery, the Vatican said.

The Pope, 71, underwent surgery at Agostino Gemelli University Policlinic in Rome on October 13 to remove a nodule from his right lung. This was determined to be pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

The surgeons removed the lower lobe of the Pope’s lung to “ensure a radical procedure; the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone, the Director of Vatican Healthcare Services, and Professor Stephano Margaritora, the lead surgeon, in a press release.

“An intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the preoperative examinations,” they said.

Pope Leo was in the operating room for 3 hours, while the operation itself lasted around 90 minutes.

The doctors noted that it was a successful operation with no complications.

According to Matteo Bruni, the Director of the Holy See Press Office, the Pope asked for dinner after the surgery and spent the evening with his secretaries and other Vatican staff.

In a press release on Wednesday, the Vatican said that the Pope’s postoperative recovery is progressing well.

According to Vatican News, Pope Leo had a calm first night following his surgery.

In the coming days, exams will be conducted on the removed tissue. There has currently been no change in the initially announced week of hospitalization.

On October 14, the Pope underwent blood tests and chest X-rays that were scheduled following his surgery. The results of these tests confirm that his postoperative recovery is progressing as expected, and the values are within a normal range for the type of operation performed.

Pope Leo has also undergone some respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking around his room, the Vatican said.

It has not yet been announced whether he will require any further treatment.

Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer globally. It accounts for around 40% of all lung cancer diagnoses.

Adenocarcinoma is a type of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which accounts for about 80–85% of all lung cancers.

Lung adenocarcinoma begins in the epithelial cells that produce mucus. It is the most common type of NSCLC.

Adenocarcinoma can be classified further by the genetic changes driving the tumor. For example, EGFR-positive lung cancer is found more often in people who have never smoked and can often be treated with targeted therapies, which is why biomarker testing of tumor tissue helps guide treatment decisions.

Treatment for NSCLC is generally determined by the stage. However, it typically involves one or a combination of:

Surgery is generally the first step in treatment for this type of lung cancer. The right lung has three lobes, or sections, and the left has two.

A doctor will often remove the entire lobe that has the tumor in order to remove the tumor and improve the outlook.

The body eventually adapts in order to compensate for the loss of function.

According to the American Cancer Society (ACS), for NSCLC that hasn’t spread outside of the lung, the 5-year relative survival rate is 67%.

Volkswagen’s upcoming electric car will be smaller and lower-priced than the ID. Polo, starting at around €20,000 ($22,500).

The new Electric Urban Car Family is the Volkswagen Group’s answer to Chinese automakers like BYD: a new lineup of compact, entry-level electric cars.

The lineup currently includes the Volkswagen ID. Polo, ID. Cross, plus the Cupra Raval and Skoda Epiq, all based on the same MEB+ platform.

After launching the lower-priced base versions of the ID. Polo and ID. Cross, starting at €24,995 and €27,995, respectively, Volkswagen is preparing to introduce an even smaller, more affordable EV in 2027.

Volkswagen revealed the ID. EVERY1 concept car last March, a preview of its upcoming entry-level EV that will arrive in 2027 starting at around €20,000.

The ID. EVERY1, which is expected to go on sale as the ID. Up! next year, is “the last piece of the puzzle,” VW brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said, as it aims to offer the widest selection in the volume segment.

With a length of 3,880 mm, the entry-level EV is positioned between the former Up! (3,600 mm) and ID. Polo (4,053 mm). Although that is tiny, VW said it will offer space for four passengers and a luggage compartment volume of 305 liters.

Volkswagen has yet to reveal details, but the €20,000 EV is expected to use the same 37 kWh LFP battery as the base ID. Polo and ID. Cross to keep costs down.

The ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery has a WLTP range of up to 334 km (207 miles), so the smaller model will likely offer around the same or slightly more range.

Volkswagen said it will offer at least 250 km (155 miles) of range. It will also use a new 70 kW (94 hp) electric motor, enabling a top speed of 130 km/h (80 mph).

The production version of the ID. EVERY1 will be one of nine new models VW plans to launch by 2027.

Volkswagen delivered on its promise to launch the ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery for under €25,000. Will it do the same with the new entry-level model at around €20,000? We will find out shortly.

It will be produced in Portugal, this has been confirmed ages ago.

According to Spanish auto magazine Autofácil, Volkswagen could manufacture the €20,000 EV in Spain, although Volkswagen has yet to confirm a production site.

The Group currently produces the ID. Polo and Cupra Raval at its Martorell plant, while the ID. Cross and Skoda Epiq are manufactured at the Navarra plant, both in Spain.

Volkswagen’s new Electric Urban Car Family is off to a promising start, securing nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June.

While those in the US will miss out on the new entry-level EV, Volkswagen is launching the ID. Tiguan in 2027 as a replacement for the ID.4.

#4882. Top 10 Issues to Consider for Polyamorous Parents

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

The popularity of divorce and nonmarital childbirth means that many people who already have children later form romantic relationships with other adults. Polyamorists and other nonmonogamous parents also form new romantic relationships. All of that means that parents need to figure out how their partners will interact with their children.

The following list is inspired by Polyam Parenting founder Jen Gerardy’s work on polyamorous parenting. A Holistic Family Consultant, breastfeeding advisor, and mediator, Gerardy helps parents juggle the commitments and emotional work of raising children in non-monogamous families. Below I condense Gerardy’s work and divide it into three sections:

1. Titles: What will we call each other? What will the child call each of us? Who gets to decide? Many polyamorous families often use the adults’ first names until otherwise noted. If the child(ren) want to call the adults something else, the kids usually create the name or nickname.

2. Affection: How are we going to express affection in front of the child? How do we show affection to the child, and how are they allowed to show affection to adults? For example, many parents prefer to allow their children to choose if they want to hug an adult or not, though some older adults can get very upset when a child refuses to hug them. How will the polycule handle it if their child does not want to hug Great Auntie Sue?

3. Time: How much time will we spend together with the child? How much time will members of the polycule spend with each other, apart from the child? Who will spend solo time with the child, and under what circumstances? Who is responsible for the child at various times? Who gets free time from parental responsibilities?

4. Daily care: How will we manage the feeding, transit, supervision, dressing, hygiene, and discipline of the children? How will the adults navigate it if someone feeds the child too much sugar or fails to make them brush their teeth? Who is responsible for overseeing the children’s daily well-being?

5. Space or housing: Who lives where, and what are the boundaries of the children’s space? What kind of space is dedicated to the adults? Who is responsible for financing, cleaning, organizing, and furnishing it? Who has their own space and who has to share? Is a partner moving into the child’s existing home? Is the child moving in with a partner? Do people live separately but spend quite a bit of time in each other’s environments? What boundaries shape the kids’ access to space?

6. Behavior: How do we behave towards each other as parents? How do we behave towards the kids? Who is responsible for the kids’ behavior? Who has the authority to enforce consequences for misbehavior?

7. Money: Who pays for the kids to go to college? Who buys their clothes, food, and housing? Who will pay for medical bills or orthodontia? How will the adults work out collaborative and/or separate money for themselves and the children?

8. Milestones: Who is invited to attend parties, birthdays, retirement events, weddings, funerals, holiday meals, and all the other holidays or events? What kinds of gifts do we give each other, and the kids? How do we present each other to others? What if some people are out as polyamorous but others are closeted?

9. Official recognition: Who is the legal representative of the children? Who can make medical and/or educational decisions? How many people can sign up to pick them up from school, and under what circumstances? Who can act as an emergency contact?

10. If the adults break up: Who is allowed to maintain contact with the children after the adults break up, and how can they do so? What circumstances do people need to retain contact with the kids and other adults in the polycule, and when do they know to cut contact with their exes? If the adults cut contact, will the children also be required to cut contact? Who has financial obligations to the children? Who has financial obligations to the other adults for raising the children (alimony)? Who has custody of the children, who is allowed visitation, and who gets to decide?

Polycules that are adding new partners to existing children’s lives or planning to have children together must consider many things. As with so many things connected to nonmonogamy, communication turns out to be a crucial ingredient when creating family boundaries. Gerardy believes that polyamorous people can have close relationships with their children and partners as long as they balance their time and energy.

“Polyamory and parenting requires self-reflection, strong boundaries, clear communication, and healthy community, but it pays dividends in fulfilling relationships for you and your kids. The first and most important step any parent, future parent, or someone dating a parent can take is to really be clear about what you need and what works for you. Do you need a lot of quiet time, or do you prefer to be surrounded by bustle? Do you want partners to be supports for the challenges of daily life, or a break from the mundane? What is important in your life beyond the roles of parent and partner? The more honestly you approach your own needs and wants, the more openly you can collaborate with potential partners on their role in your children's lives.”

Obviously, there are more than 10 issues for any parent to explore, and that is true here as well. Exploring these issues before having children, or as early in a dating relationship as possible, can help alleviate future stress.
