#4850. sonnen files for insolvency in Germany as US sales double

Residential battery storage maker sonnen is reporting two very different stories today: Its German business has filed for insolvency, while sonnen USA says sales have doubled and it’s preparing to expand.

The insolvency filing comes just two months after Shell sold sonnen to investment group TIVEN. Germany’s Handelsblatt reported that sonnen GmbH confirmed the filing and informed roughly 400 employees in Wildpoldsried, Bavaria, on October 22.

For homeowners with sonnen batteries, the immediate question is what happens to service. According to Handelsblatt, the company intends to keep supporting its more than 150,000 existing customers. But a substantial overhaul is coming: Numerous subsidiaries are expected to be wound down or enter insolvency proceedings under self-administration, with only one production site remaining. The report does not identify that site.

Meanwhile, sonnen USA’s announcement describes a growing home battery business. The company says sales have doubled and production has tripled year over year, supported by expanded manufacturing in Stone Mountain, Georgia. It expects to deliver more than 180 megawatt-hours of residential battery storage in 2026.

Much of that growth comes from virtual power plants (VPPs). These connect home batteries so they can work together to support the grid, giving households another way to earn value from their solar and storage systems.

In Texas, sonnen says its SOLRITE offering serves more than 6,000 homes, combining rooftop solar, batteries, energy management, and VPP participation. In Massachusetts, its sonnenCommunity program offers cash rewards to participating homeowners in National Grid and Eversource territories. The company also reports rising sales through its Wattsmart program in Utah.

TIVEN bought the entire global business, including sonnen USA. US CEO Blake Richetta stated today that “TIVEN is firmly committed to the long-term success of sonnen USA as a strong, market-leading company in the North American VPP energy market.”

TIVEN stated that it “looks forward to bolstering the company’s impressive growth.”

But the US announcement leaves an important question unanswered: How will the German restructuring affect the US operation and its customers? It doesn’t address the insolvency filing, and sonnen USA declined to comment on developments in Germany when contacted by pv magazine.

The US growth figures show demand for sonnen’s batteries. What customers still need is a clear explanation of how manufacturing, software support, and service will be maintained through the restructuring.

#4849. Is There Alcohol in Non-Alcoholic Drinks?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

The popularity of “alcohol-free” beverages has grown worldwide.1 When seeing the labels “alcohol-free”, “non-alcoholic”, and “dealcoholized,” on beverages, it is important to understand what they mean to make informed decisions about whether to drink them and how much. While these low-alcohol labels suggest very low to no alcohol content, the true meaning of these labels may surprise you and change how you choose to consume these beverages.

As it turns out, the meaning of these low-alcohol labels depends on where you live.2 In most countries, the label a manufacturer is allowed to use on their product is determined by a centralized government body (e.g., Canadian Food Inspection Agency, United States (U.S.) Food and Drug Administration (FDA) or Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB)). Each government body determines which labels may be used based on the alcohol by volume (ABV) of the beverage. For context, the typical ABV for beer is 5%, for wine is 12%, and for distilled spirits is 40%.

While there are regulated processes for these low-alcohol labels on beverages, the actual ABV requirements differ between (and even within) countries. In the U.S., the maximum for the “dealcoholized” label is 0.5% ABV. “Non-alcoholic beverages” can contain traces of alcohol (less than 0.5% ABV), but an “alcohol-free” beverage must have no detectable alcohol (0% ABV). In contrast, in Canada, a “dealcoholized” beverage can contain up to 1.1% ABV. Further, the labels “non-alcoholic” and “alcohol-free” are used interchangeably for products with alcohol levels up to 0.05% ABV.

When making decisions about whether to drink these beverages (and how much), these distinctions between drink labels can be vitally important. Many people wish to avoid consuming alcohol entirely. Common reasons for not drinking alcohol at all are cultural and religious reasons, cancer prevention (alcohol is a carcinogen and increases risk for cancer), and improving mental health or well-being. For instance, the distinction between having alcohol in a beverage (even small amounts) versus not can be critical for someone who has chosen to stop drinking alcohol completely to help manage their alcohol use disorder. Further, underage consumption of these beverages is a potential concern. In many cases, underage purchasing and consumption are unregulated. While it is very unlikely that the ABV of these beverages would contribute to underage intoxication, early exposure to low-alcohol beverages that taste and look like typical alcoholic beverages may encourage young people to drink alcohol more heavily and at younger ages (increasing risk of alcohol problems).

For some people, the differences in ABV between these labels may not be as important. For instance, someone who wishes to reduce how much alcohol they drink, but not stop entirely, can meet that goal by replacing their typical alcoholic drink with a drink with any of these low-alcohol labeled beverages. This is because “dealcoholized”, “alcohol-free”, and “non-alcoholic” beverages should all have much lower ABV than typical alcoholic drinks. Similarly, switching completely to drinks with these labels will likely avoid intoxication. Intoxication typically occurs after drinking two to three typical alcoholic drinks in an hour. Given that these beverages have substantially reduced levels of alcohol, it would require drinking a considerable amount of these beverages in a short amount of time to become intoxicated. There are exceptions to this idea. In countries where these labels apply to beverages with lowered ABV, but not very low ABV, someone could still become intoxicated if they drank enough of them in a relatively short period of time. For instance, drinking four to five “deacloholized” beverages within an hour (at the upper end of 1.0% ABV limit in Canada) could result in a similar intoxication level to drinking one typical alcoholic beverage during that timeframe.

Taken together, beverages labeled as low-alcohol offer a promising alternative to consuming typical alcoholic beverages. They can be a useful substitute beverage when someone wishes to reduce their alcohol use. Depending on whether you want to reduce or stop your alcohol use entirely, it may be worthwhile taking a closer look at what those labels mean where you live and being informed about how much alcohol may be in that beverage to ensure the beverage will help you meet that goal.

1. World Health Organization (2023). A public health perspective on zero and low-alcohol beverages (Snapshot series on alcohol control policies and practice). Brief 10. Geneva. Licence: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO.

2. Burton, R., Angus, K., Morgan, A., Howell, R., Critchlow, N., Kersbergen, I., ... & Fitzgerald, N. (2026). Regulation of alcohol‐free and low‐alcohol drinks: Learning from a comparative analysis of eight countries. Drug and Alcohol Review, 45(3), e70126.

#4848. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep issues, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:

Research shows that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” said Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” said Pier.

#4847. Another megawatt-level charger enters China: 300 miles in 5 minutes

Chery has announced a 1.44 megawatt charging system, able to deliver 500km (311 miles) in 5 minutes. And it’s not even the fastest system available in China.

It’s become common knowledge at this point that Chinese EVs are the world’s state of the art, but the country isn’t sitting on its laurels, it’s still racing to compete with newer and better technology.

A case in point has been the country’s DC fast chargers, where we’ve seen a slew of announcements of new systems in just the last year.

BYD has a 1.5MW charger which it has already installed 10,000 of, Geely just announced a 2.2MW charger, and CATL has a hyper-fast charging battery.

The competition is so fierce that firms are starting to compete over seconds, not minutes of charging time.

And now, a new challenger appears: Chery.

Chery announced a 1.44MW charger that can add 500km (311miles) of range to a battery in 5 minutes, and can charge from 10-97% in 6 minutes and 50 seconds, as reported by CarNewsChina.

The numbers put it in league with the best of the best in the country. Per CarNewsChina’s accounting, the new Chery “Volt-Dragon” battery is the second-fastest at reaching 97% state of charge, 23 seconds behind CATL’s 6 minute, 27 second record time. FAW, Geely and BYD are all between 8 and 9 minutes for the same full charge metric.

Some other firms released times for charging in very cold or very warm weather, which Chery declined to release during its announcement. Though it did say that it could still deliver 500km of range in 8 minutes in “conservative scenarios.”

Could it be the drugged out Elon Musk is more into politics and taking over the world than advancing EV technology at an electric car company.

In Chery’s announcement, it dropped the same buzzword as Geely did: “AI-Powered.” Chery calls its system CheryMind, and supposedly it adjusts charging power based on temperature changes within the battery, to help maintain optimal charging speeds and battery health.

Meanwhile in the US, the fastest public chargers are around 400kW, with 750kW potentially coming next year. That’s all plenty quick enough for refueling, especially on a roadtrip, but for high-throughput DC charging locations, especially those in urban areas where some people might not have a consistent parking spot to charge in (and yes, we need to fix that), higher speed chargers can relieve a lot of pressure.

Chery has only just started installing chargers, and says it will have 100 chargers open in 10 Chinese cities soon. It plans to install 20,000 stations worldwide by 2029, which is quite a bit slower than BYD’s target to have 20,000 chargers installed by the end of this year.

#4846. Ultra Muscular = Fake? Addressing Male Body Image Concerns

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

A common stereotype is that appearance concerns are a "woman’s thing," and men simply don’t worry as much about their looks. The taboo around men speaking about their body concerns certainly doesn’t help: Without speaking about them, men are less likely to receive support, and we continue to assume that men just aren’t as worried about their bodies.

Yet, research shows that many men do experience body concerns, and the percentage of men who worry about their bodies has been increasing in recent years, particularly among young people. This is a serious problem because, like body concerns among women, body concerns among men may lead to mental health risks, such as disordered eating, excessive exercise, anxiety, and low self-esteem. Motivated by the need to address body concerns among men, my colleagues and I at Maastricht University conducted an experiment to test a novel, computer-based intervention technique.

In our experiment, young men (18-29 years old) were tested individually at our lab. First, they completed questionnaires to measure how they were thinking and feeling about their bodies. Then, they were randomly assigned to complete either the intervention technique or a "placebo" technique, both completed via the computer.

Participants who received the intervention technique where they were repeatedly shown images of men who represented today’s "ideal male body"—namely, young men with lean, ultra-muscular bodies. They were also shown images of sports items (e.g., tennis racket) or neutral items (e.g., stapler). After each image appeared on the screen, they were instructed to click on the image as quickly as possible, and then a word would appear. The images of the ultra-muscular men were always followed by negative words like fake, unnatural, and artificial. In contrast, the sports items were always followed by sports-related words (e.g., net), and the neutral items were always followed by color-related words (e.g., green). Participants completed this sequence—viewing an image, clicking on it, seeing a word—more than 300 times in rapid succession.

The idea behind this seemingly simple computer task is based on fundamental principles in psychology. In brief, repeatedly pairing idealized bodies with negative words should create a more negative association with the male body ideal. As a result, participants should be less likely to view these idealized bodies as appropriate standards of comparison, and should feel less negatively about their own bodies. Further, we focused the intervention technique on images of the male body ideal based on the wealth of research showing that they are a key factor contributing to body concerns among men.

Participants who received the "placebo" technique completed a computer task where they viewed the same images and words; however, the words following each image were random, so there was no systematic association between any image or word category.

After the computer task, all participants again completed questionnaires about how they were thinking and feeling about their bodies. Importantly, participants had not been informed that the experiment was about an intervention technique to reduce body concerns. In this way, we could minimize the risk that participants might answer the questionnaires based on how they expected we would want them to answer the questionnaires.

After collecting all of our data, we used men’s questionnaire scores to analyze whether there was a change in men’s thoughts and feelings about their bodies from before to after the computer task—and, importantly, whether this change was significantly different between the intervention and placebo group.

Our main finding is that men who completed the intervention technique, compared to men who completed the placebo technique, reported an increase in muscle appearance satisfaction from before to after the computer task. We did not find any significant changes in one of our other key outcomes, self-objectification (i.e., the tendency to view one’s body from an appearance-based perspective).

Our experiment provides first evidence that repeatedly pairing images of the male body ideal with negative words (fake, unnatural, artificial) can lead to reductions in body concerns among young men. Specifically, the intervention technique led to an immediate increase in muscle appearance satisfaction. Potentially, creating a more negative association with the male body ideal may have compromised these images as appropriate sources of body comparisons, leading men to feel more satisfied with their own bodies.

Importantly, this experiment was a first, "proof of concept" study into whether this intervention technique holds promise. Testing this intervention technique again in other samples of men—ideally with longer follow-up measurements—will be important. If the technique continues to prove effective, it may be a useful complement to other larger-scale interventions for men’s body concerns. It will also be important to investigate how this technique can be integrated into men’s daily lives, where they are continuously confronted with images of the male body ideal, for example on social media. We look forward to conducting other research into men’s body image and future avenues for treatment.

Martijn, C., Steenhuis, M., Ammernick, A., Balzer, J., Haimüller, J., & Alleva, J. M. (2026). Muscular= Fake? Testing a Picture‐Word Pairing Procedure to Increase Muscle Appearance Satisfaction in Young Men. European Eating Disorders Review.

#4845. The 58 Best New Shows of 2026 (and 2 More We Can't Wait For)

We've got murder mysteries, stories of love and lust, and lots and lots of Yellowstone. And that's just the beginning.

THE IDEA OF "new" television shows is a little bit of a tricky one these days. Sure, we do still get a fair share of truly new, exciting, unique ideas each year—just look at shows like Severance a couple years ago and Pluribus last year. Shows like last year's The Lowdown—rich, well-written, character-focused stories—still draw major stars like Ethan Hawke and still hit in a big way for audiences that watch it. If someone was being dramatic and wanted to say original TV was dead, dying, or on life support, there's plenty of evidence out there to throw in their face.

But at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong. For one reason or another, so much of the TV landscape—even shows we're really excited for—are based around something that in one way or another already exists.

Look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something new, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV. Which is why we kind of have two different options here—people need to be really trusting of word of mouth and really aware when something is a really good new, original show (because no one likes to waste their time with a piece of junk), and we just need to really hope that all the remakes, reboots, reimaginings, and re-whatevers are good.

And they should be! HBO's Lanterns is modeled after True Detective, stars Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre as the titular Green Lanterns, and counts Watchmen genius Damon Lindelof as a producer. Of course it’s good. Below, we're going to keep track all year. We're charting the shows we already know are good. We're charting the shows we think might be good. And we're charting the shows that may not even come out this year, but if they do... they still might not be good. But, again, say it with us: We're choosing to be hopeful.

Netflix has been really good of late at the pulpy, potboiler, limited series, and His & Hers is the latest in that winning streak. The show follows a detective (Jon Bernthal) and his estranged journalist wife (Tessa Thompson) as they both hunt for answers when a local woman—whom they both have a close connection to—winds up dead. Based on Alice Feeney's book of the same name, His & Hers is exactly how this kind of show should be: Juicy, fun, easy to watch, and filled with really good actors.

In shrinking its story down to a more intimate one that takes place between the margins of major universe events, Game of Thrones takes a page out of the Andor handbook with A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (based on George R.R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas). This short series, which follows a big, humble, anxious hedge knight (former professional rugby playerPeter Claffey)and his little friend/squire (Dexter Sol Ansell) is a true breath of fresh air for Thrones fans on both a story and character level. It's a delight.

Doesn't the premise of Ponies just sound fun? This spy series set in '70s Moscow follows a pair of women working with the CIA who find themselves at the midst of a vast conspiracy when their husbands both die under mysterious circumstances. And those women are played by The White Lotus's Haley Lu Richardson and Game of Thrones queen Emilia Clarke. Sometimes something that sounds like a winner just turns out to be one.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins (NBC/Peacock)

This show about a disgraced former football player (Tracy Morgan) and a documentary filmmaker following him (Daniel Radcliffe) comes from the team behind 30 Rock, so you know you're going to get several jokes per minute. Plus, Morgan and Radcliffe are no slouches themselves. The show had a special debut in January and will continue on a regular schedule later in February.

At the very least, Wonder Man is among the best shows Marvel ever made—and you could make a case that it's at the top of the list. Yahya Abdul Mateen II plays the titular hero (aka actor Simon Williams) as the kind of guy we love to love in this sort of story: humble, well-meaning, charismatic, and ambitious. But when he meets fellow actor (and former fake terrorist) Trevor Slattery (Ben Kingsley) and learns that his favorite movie from childhood is being remade by an acclaimed director, everything changes. Wonder Man isn't just a good Marvel show, but a good show about people, movies, and friendship period. Let's hope the MCU takes notes from what worked so well here and keeps the streak going in the future.

One of America's great cultural institutions made its grand return in 2026: The Muppet Show! This version—coming from executive producers Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg—is directly modeled on the original Muppet Show, which means special guests, musical performances, comedy sketches, and lots of fun. The first episode, which featured special guest star Sabrina Carpenter, was an absolute delight for anyone who likes Kermit, Miss Piggy, and friends (or who just likes laughing and having a good time). For now, it's just this one episode, but if the reaction is strong enough (and it seems like it might be), the show will come back in full.

The latest entry in producer Ryan Murphy's American Story universe is called Love Story, and follows the romance and life between Carolyn Bessette Kennedy and John F. Kennedy Jr. The show is, however, much better than that tabloid-y description sounds; Sarah Pidgeon, who plays Carolyn, is a star, coming off her Tony-nominated role in the Fleetwood Mac-inspired play Stereophonic. But Paul Anthony Kelly, who plays JFK Jr., is a real discovery—it's his first role (he was previously a model), and he truly feels like a reincarnation of the late attorney/magazine publisher/dashing public figure. Of course, this is a story that ends in an extreme tragedy—so if you get invested, be sure to have your tissues ready.

This wild documentary series looks at different disputes between neighbors, telling compelling and often escalating true stories that will truly floor you in the depiction of their very-real truth. Think about this less as a story about the legalities of these disputes, and more a look into some larger-than-life characters through an often trippy, absurd lens. The series is produced by Josh Safdie and Ronald Bronstein, coming off of their recent success on the Oscar-nominated Marty Supreme.

The new season of Scrubs brings back almost all of the original cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, and Sarah Chalke. And audiences who love and/or remember that trio and most of the show's original dramedy premise should be pleased with this new version of the beloved aughts sitcom. The last season aired in 2010, so we're OK with calling this 16-years-later revival a 'new' show.

DTF St. Louis follows trio of languishing adults—played by the electric trio of Jason Bateman, Linda Cardellini, and David Harbour—who get involved in a love triangle and general madness that results in one of them winding up dead. You may think you have an idea of what you're getting into with this show based on the cast and that premise, but believe us—all of your expectations will be upended. DTF St. Louis is a tonal balancing act, a show that bounces between hilarious dark comedy, compelling mystery, and gutting, relatable drama. It's one of the best shows of the year.

The second age of Yellowstone begins in earnest with Marshals, a 13-episode drama that airs on CBS (and streams on Parmaount+ either simultaneously or a day later, depending on which tier of subscription you have). The series focuses on Luke Grimes's character Kayce, and how an old SEAL Team leader (Logan Marshall-Green) recruits him into his Marshal squad. There's at least one more Yellowstone spinoff coming in 2026—Dutton Ranch—and so this is the one leading the charge.

One of the busiest men in show business these days—on both the big and small screen—is Guy Ritchie, and his newest endeavor takes him back to a world he's inhabited a couple times before. Young Sherlock follows, well, a Young Sherlock Holmes. And as you can imagine, it follows Arthur Conan Doyle's famous detective as he solves a mystery. Hero Fiennes Tiffin plays the titular character, and Colin Firth is also part of the show's cast. If you're into that, you'll have a fun time! It's an enjoyable show.

The erotic thriller is back! Or, well, juicy erotic character study dramedy? Whatever we want to call it, Netflix's Vladimir is one of the year's most exciting new shows. Based on the novel of the same name, this show follows a longtime literature professor at a college (Rachel Weisz, constantly breaking the fourth wall) who finds herself in the midst of controversy when her fellow professor husband (John Slattery) gets caught sleeping with students. She takes this as an opportunity to switch things up a bit, and so she becomes smitten with her very sexy new colleague (Leo Woodall). It's a fun, zippy, juicy time—and kind of like if Deadpool was actually about a smart woman in academia who's spinning her wheels and maybe just a little bit horny.

From the mold of Ted Lasso and Shrinking comes Rooster, which stars Steve Carell and counts Lasso and Shrinking co-creator Bill Lawrence (who also made Scrubs and Cougar Town) as its showrunner. Carell plays an author who heads to help his professor daughter on a college campus... and becomes enamored with life there. Imagine Back to School but with some middle-age soul-searching and academia at play? Sure! HBO's got another winner on their hands with this one—and maybe Carell can get the Emmy that he somehow never got for The Office.

There are 29 books in the Scarpetta series, and, now, one TV show on Prime Video starring Nicole Kidman and Jamie Lee Curtis. The series follows forensic pathologist Dr. Kay Scarpetta (Kidman) as she solves a crime—but the show is so much more than just that. In a way, Scarpetta is destined to fit into Prime Video's roster of rock-solid procedural murder mysteries, which also includes Reacher, Cross, Bosch, and plenty more. But it's got a little bit of an extra chaotic oomph—helped out by the star-studded cast that also includes Bobby Cannavale and Simon Baker—that make it worth your while and a unique, fun show.

Sunny Nights, which aired in Australia last year, now makes its U.S. debut on Hulu. The premise is simple: A pair of siblings (played by the very funny Will Forte and D'Arcy Carden) want to start a spray tan business, but wind up entrenched in the criminal underworld. Whoops! Forte and Carden have been two of our finest comedic actors for a while—with ability to play depth in addition to that humor—and the show thrives when they're at their strongest. A solid watch for anyone looking for something light but compelling.

This series—from Yellowstone super writer/producer Taylor Sheridan—follows Stacy Clyburn (Michelle Pfeiffer) and her family, as they move from the busy, stressful world of New York City to a more rustic setting out in beautiful Montana after a totally unforseen tragedy. Kurt Russellplays her husband, Preston, with his usual endless charisma, while the supporting cast includes the likes of Matthew Fox and Suits star Patrick J. Adams. Sheridan does his usual zigging and zagging in The Madison—the tone can sometimes shift from very sad to zany and comedic, and, as usual, there's a bit of social commentary speechifying buried in almost every scene. But if you're on board with the writing style he uses in shows like Yellowstone and Landman, you'll probably be OK with it here, especially if you're ready for a heavier and more contemplative tone. This show was originally planned to be part of the Yellowstone connected universe, but those plans have since been changed; It's now a new story, but with that Montana setting, you still get to look at all sorts of beautiful landscapes.

After striking gold a couple years ago with Jury Duty, Prime Video gives its grand Truman Show-esque experiment another try with a second season called Company Retreat. This time around, we follow a regular guy who thinks he’s working as a temp for a hot sauce company and joining them on their annual company bonding retreat. Of course, everyone around him is actually an actor in a scripted, engineered situation. It’s a little goofier than the first season, but seeing how everything plays out is compelling, often very funny television nonetheless. A worthy follow-up, and, honestly, we might just watch these as long as they feel like making them.

Riz Ahmed is the creator and star of Bait, a show about an actor who thinks he's about to get offered the role of a lifetime—James Bond!—and the madness that spirals out of such a revelation. If you're a fan of Ahmed's (and why wouldn't you be?) this will be a fun ride.

Something Very Bad Is Going To Happen (Netflix)

Camila Morrone (Daisy Jones and the Six) and Adam DiMarco(The White Lotus) are set to get married in this horror series from showrunner Haley Z. Boston (who worked on the very underrated Brand New Cherry Flavor) and producers The Duffer Brothers. And not to oversell, but Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen is the best horror show I've seen in quite some time. While the show plays with familiar settings and tropes—you may think of Ready or Not or Midsommar during the show's eight episodes—it's so filled with Ari Aster-esque dread and stunning, striking camera work that it doesn't even matter. Horror fans are in for an absolute treat with this one.

#4843. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4842. Why Being the Mom of a Gay Son Matters

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

I am standing at the back of a darkened room. On the screen, a documentary is being shown. And throughout the room, people in the audience are openly laughing, weeping, murmuring. I can't tell you what this moment, and all the other moments like it, mean to me.

The film being shown is the documentary I produced and directed, called Mom, I Have Something to Tell You. It shares interviews I've conducted with a plethora of gay men and their mothers, talking about their relationships, uncovering hidden thoughts and reactions, and telling a story I've been helping people tell for over 10 years.

The only thing that even equaled the feeling I had that night was when the documentary made its debut on YouTube. It has since garnered more than 35,000 views and collected comments that have made me, too, weep.

I had a feeling this topic would be meaningful and exciting for other people—and is it ever! Sharing the stories of women and their gay sons, which no one had done before, evokes powerful reactions: some chuckle, some tear up, some recite long stories about how this relationship is so powerful. I frequently forget to bring tissues with me—which is a mistake.

I knew I had to capture the stories in video form—rather than writing them up like I usually do—so others could see for themselves what happens here. I wanted to share the depths of these stories, not just describe them. Every time I filmed or shared snippets, the reactions of others—on Instagram, Facebook, Tik-Tok, and YouTube—emphasized was why this is so important.

I've never met a gay man who had an easy childhood. Gay boys are nearly universally discriminated against, ignored, bullied, or even abused. What I hear from these men is that the impact of a mother who is supportive, nurturing, and who defends her child makes a tremendous difference in their later well-being.

When one of these men is given the opportunity to tell their mothers, directly, what a difference their love and support has made in their life, something magical happens for both of them. He's able to express his gratitude and love; she's able to see what was often a thankless and difficult decision as a courageous and life-affirming act.

And audiences? We all have relationships with our parents and children that are often left unexamined, and the film becomes a prism through which everyone can find their own story.

All of this was the result of my own clinical work with gay men. I was noticing how important their relationships with their mothers were. Interested, I did a literature search on the subject, coming up with...nothing. No one was interested in exploring it. So I did.

Without literature on the subject, I started to explore the relationship myself, interviewing gay men and their mothers, sometimes alone, sometimes together, until I felt I was starting to build a real body of information and a useful resource. I founded a nonprofit called Gay Sons & Mothers, and was surprised to see how much people appreciated having someone pay attention to something that was obviously of critical significance to them.

At first, it was just me: Those early days found me lugging equipment around from interview to interview, worrying about whether the microphones were picking up our voices or whether I'd remembered to turn on the video (once or twice, I hadn't); I finally hired a videographer so I could focus on the content and the people. It was, for sure, a journey of discovery. And the result, for now, is Mom, I Have Something to Tell You.

Time after time gay men have told me how their mothers enabled them to find their voice and their place, showed them that they were not deficient, and encouraged them to be fully themselves. These are mothers who stood up to spouses, families, cultures, and communities to protect their sons. Who bought their boys dolls and told them they were perfect just as they were. Who advocated for their children, risking everything themselves to stand up for what—and who—was important.

Shouldn't that be a relationship that's celebrated?

One example is that of the "Mama Dragons," a group of women who belong to the Church of Latter-Day Saints. These women loved their gay sons with their whole hearts and found themselves needing to reconcile that love with being part of a church and community that didn't recognize the value of their children.

Eventually, as I met so many of these courageous women, I began recording a video series called Mothers Who Inspire, talking with mothers of gay sons about their challenges and joys. A particularly poignant segment was my interview with Judy Shepard, who created the Matthew Shepard Foundation in memory of her murdered son.

Here's just one example: When David first heard of Gay Sons & Mothers, it opened floodgates of emotion about his own relationship with his mother. They clearly loved each other, but he'd never dared come out to her; he assumed she inferred it, and didn't want to risk bringing it into the open. But watching the film gave him the courage he needed to talk with her about his identity for the first time in 20 years. So it's no exaggeration to say the organization and film have changed lives.

I've shared these stories with medical communities, at young people’s events, with artists’ associations, and with professional organizations and workplaces. The presentation content and length is tailored to the specific audience, with question-and-answer and discussion segments available.

One of my favorite encounters was at a mental-health conference where I offered a workshop. A 78-year-old psychiatrist had driven four hours to attend my workshop, and during the sharing time, he said, "I never imagined in my lifetime I'd say this—but I am gay." The group went wild. It was one of my first presentations and his response—and that of the group as a whole—told me I was on the right path.

The impact of the film is shown clearly through the comments. "Brings back lots of memories growing up with my loving and accepting mother," writes one viewer. "We didn't even need to talk about it. I treasure those great memories seeing this video of mothers and their gay sons."

Another viewer said, "I knew my son was gay from the age of three. He howled when I gifted my niece a Marie Antoinette satin dress for Xmas, he so desperately wanted to wear it himself. I had to promise to buy him a Barbie instead!"

Echoing what I wrote about in a recent Unwrapped essay about having "extra" mothers, one viewer said, "My grandmother was the most important person in my life (...) I knew I was gay when I was around eight and my nan was never homophobic, she would drop remarks like 'you're special' and 'we love you' (...) she was my safe space. We never had a coming-out moment, as she would ask about any boys I liked."

All this confirms the impact that others' stories have on us and how they allow us to recapture the women who have made our present lives possible.

This is just the beginning: As we expand to the next generation, it's increasingly important that mothers receive the validation and recognition they deserve in order to feel supported and to be the best they can for their kids. Go check out Mom, I Have Something to Tell You, and see if you don't agree.

#4841. Overhead wired charging comes to Austin electric bus fleet

CapMetro’s Austin transit fleets electrified two public bus lines and opened two new park-and-ride facilities featuring overhead pantograph-style wired charging equipment to help Austinites breathe a little bit easier.

Originally announced in June, CapMetro’s two new park-and-ride stations are now open. Dubbed the Goodnight Ranch and Expo Center facilities debuted alongside the agency’s Rapid 800 and 837 electric bus routes, adding upgraded passenger amenities and end-of-line charging infrastructure to support its growing fleet of electric transit buses.

At CapMetro’s main bus depot, infrastructure partner Camber Charging supplied and installed two 1,440 kW charging systems connected to 48 industrial dispensers. The installation provides 2.9 MW of total charging capacity, and is designed to support overnight charging for up to 48 electric buses simultaneously.

The new Goodnight Ranch and Expo Center terminals extend that infrastructure along the Rapid 800 and 837 routes with the overhead pantograph chargers that are the big news here, allowing buses to top off their batteries at the end of each line and eliminate any lingering range anxiety for the trip back.

“Instead of a typical bus holding 8 hours of charging, on-route charging takes that out to 20 to 22 hours,” explains CapMetro Chief Operations Officer and Executive VP, Andy Skabowski. “Every time that pantograph drops, we charge that bus. That’s what makes a commitment like (every) 10- to 15-minute service possible.”

The buses themselves are built on Canadian manufacturer New Flyer’s Xcelsior battery-electric transit platform (battery specs aren’t included in the release, but New Flyer claims up to 660 kWh of available capacity). And, with up to 320 all-electric hp with all its torque available at 0 rpm, the city’s 48 electric buses will have no problem navigating Austin’s stop-and-go traffic.

This seems like a logical cost effective solution. In theory, this should enable transit systems to purchase busses with smaller batteries which would surely offset the cost of the new charging infrastructure.

Camber Charging provides preventive maintenance, charger and energy management software and remote diagnostics across all three locations.

EVERYONE KNOWS THAT Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson are one of the great duos in show business. After meeting and becoming friends on the set of the 1999 comedy film EdTV, the actors began a long friendship, along the way collaborating again for the first season of True Detective, widely considered to be one of the great television shows of all time.

But did you know that in addition to being great friends, the two might also be half-relatives? That’s the premise of Apple TV’s new comedy series Brothers, which reunites the duo on screen for the first time since 2014’s True Detective, and pulls from a bit of very real mythology that the two only relatively recently discovered on their own. “Matthew’s mother, I’d known her 25 years, and she told me, ‘I knew your father.’ You know, like, with the ellipses: ‘I knew… your father’” Harrelson told Variety. “She tells me, and I’m thinking, ‘What’s behind this story?’ And then I find out they weren’t just friends—there was a little more to it.”

Brothers, in turn, stars McConaughey and Harrelson as fictional versions of themselves exploring this possibility. Think of it as the meta-nature of Curb Your Enthusiasm, combined with the goofiness of a family sitcom like Schitt’s Creek or Malcolm in the Middle, and, of course, the star power of True Detective.

Now, just because they made the show doesn’t mean that McConaughey believes the story. “Woody thinks he knows that we’re brothers, and it’s not that I don’t want to know—I don’t believe it,” McConaughey told Variety at the show’s premiere. “My mom’s the one who started this whole damn thing, by saying ‘I knew… your father… with the long pause after that. Even my five-year-old son understood the innuendo of what that meant.”

So, are the A-listers actually brothers? You figure they could just take a DNA test and figure out once and for all. But for now, that doesn’t seem to be in the cards. “I’ve been wanting to, but he refuses,” Harrelson told The Hollywood Reporter. McConaughey then added that maybe that could change in the future—but he’s a little frightened about what it could mean. “I’ll probably come around to it,” he said. “If it’s true, I’ve got a lot to unpack. If it’s not true, he’s not going to be near as fun to hang out with.”

There’s a lot to figure out for these two. But in the meantime, why not see how fictional Matthew and Woody handle it? Below, we’ve got all the information to make sure you don’t miss an episode of Apple TV’s Brothers.

The debut season of Brothers will run for eight episodes, with episodes rolling out on a weekly basis, the first seven of which have now aired. That means there’s still one more week—and one episodes of Matthew and Woody’s brotherly (or not-so-brotherly) chaos—remaining in the show’s first season.

#4839. How Pathological Narcissism Erodes the Best of Relationships

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Being able to trust your partner to want the best for you forms the bedrock of a close relationship. No one wants a romantic partner who constantly engages in sabotage and deception. So what happens when people discover that their partner turns out to be doing just that?

Consider Betty and Francis, who started dating a year ago, having met online. Betty always felt that Francis was a bit on the overly competitive side, turning everything into a battle for victory. If Betty succeeded at work on some small achievement, Francis refused to take it seriously. Betty decided to stick it out because Francis seems to need her there and often relies on her for support. But warning signs like these are making her think that maybe she’d better get out while she still can.

As pointed out in a new study by Saint Camillus International University’s Guyonne Rogier and colleagues (2026), “trust appears to be one of the most desired features in a partner.” They key component of trust, they go on to note, is faith, or the confidence that a partner will remain caring and helpful regardless of what may happen in the future. It’s this uncertainty factor that could prove to be the hardest for narcissistic individuals to accept. But it’s not just any narcissistic individual; vulnerable narcissists should be particularly unhappy with the uncertainty factor. They don’t want to risk any possible rejection or disappointment from their partner.

Narcissism alone, even the vulnerable form, isn’t the only factor that can destroy faith and, hence, relationships. Rogier et al. point out that highly narcissistic people approach relationships from the two dimensions of admiration and rivalry. They are afraid of being outdone by their partner, because this would threaten their sense of worth. The activation of feelings of rivalry sets off the chain of reactions that ultimately leads faith to fall by the wayside.

The Italian authors tested this potential set of mechanisms by building a model that started with vulnerable narcissism as the origin of feelings of rivalry. In turn, rivalry toward the partner would lead, the model predicted, to the outcome of loss of faith in the romantic partner. Although this was a correlational study, the authors were able to test their model using controlled statistical modeling.

The online sample of more than 4,000 Italian adults (average age of 32 years) completed a set of standard personality questionnaires. Faith was measured with items such as “Even if I don’t know how my partner will react, I feel comfortable telling him/her anything about myself, even the things I am ashamed of” (reverse-scored). To measure vulnerable narcissism, the authors used the corresponding scale from the Narcissism Personality Inventory, with items such as “Sometimes I avoid people because I fear they will disappoint me.” Finally, rivalry was assessed with three subscales from the Narcissism Admiration and Rivalry Questionnaire (NARQ): Devaluation (“Other people are worth nothing”), Supremacy (“I want my rivals to fail”), and Aggressiveness (“I get annoyed when someone steals the attention from me”).

Consistent with the authors’ prediction, grandiose but not vulnerable narcissism predicted lack of faith in the partner. Grandiose narcissists may rival their partners, but they feel confident in how “magnificent and unique” they are, which should ensure their partner’s “love and devotion.” Vulnerable narcissists, anxiously attached to their partners, don’t have this same level of confidence in their ability. This leads the narcissistic rivalry to emerge, much as has happened to Betty and Francis.

Tracing the trajectory of relationships for people high in vulnerable narcissism from the study’s results reinforces this idea. In a good relationship, faith develops over time as the partners become less fearful of rejection even if they show their weak side. In relationships with vulnerable narcissists, rivalry builds over time. They start to devalue and distrust their partner the more they reveal their flaws and limitations. The rivalry becomes increasingly aggressive as a means of self-protection.

If you’ve been in a situation like Betty’s, you can understand the push and pull that she might be experiencing. You can feel bad for a vulnerable narcissist whose precarious sense of self seems to need constant reinforcing. But when this person starts to attack you, this tries your patience. It can even make you start to question your own self-worth.

Pinpointing the problem in the maladaptive quality of narcissistic rivalry could provide you with important insights. The vulnerable narcissist may not “want” to be nasty, but may be unable to control the aggressive attempts to put you down. The flip side of rivalry is admiration. The grandiose narcissist may have too much of this feeling of self-satisfaction and superiority, but the vulnerable narcissist may need a bit more.

Returning to the primary purpose of the study, it can also be helpful to think about the faith dimension. A person high in vulnerable narcissism never feels certain of the future, which includes the certainty that a romantic partner will remain faithful. This can lead to endless worry but also endless attempts to win any battle for superiority.

To sum up, life with a pathological narcissist is never very pleasant. If you care about this person, though, understanding how rivalry breeds lack of faith can help you intervene before the dynamics take a toll on your relationship.

Rogier, G., Falbo, M. C., Zinesi, L., & Velotti, P. (2026). Is the link between pathological narcissism and poor romantic trust explained by rivalry? Journal of Couple & Relationship Therapy. https://doi.org/10.1080/15332691.2026.2719440

#4838. Yozma IN 11 review: The OG mini e-moto gets updates galore

…including 4.5kW motor, bigger 1.4kWh battery and 45mph top speed

Yozma may not have invented the mini moto space, but they certainly helped mainstream it. Together with Tuttios and Sur Rons, Yozma’s IN10 was one of the most popular mini motos out there, and if you surveyed the average group of 14-15-year-olds in a suburban rideout, you’d be hard-pressed not to find at least a few Yozma IN10s among them…

Today Yozma is shipping the IN 11 ($100 off with code 9TO5TOYS100), which attempts to bridge the gap between entry-level mini-bikes and high-end off-roaders, but at what cost?

Taken in a vacuum, the Yozma IN11 is an impressive update to the IN 10 and actually is more closely specced to the bigger IN10 Pro.

But we of course, don’t live in a vacuum, and others, including the Heybike Villain and the Engwe Eagle have already brought 52V, 4.5kW motors to the pit bike form factor, sometimes at much lower cost.

I should say here that parents who want to keep their kids’ e-motos in the 20-30mph range are going to be a whole lot happier with the 2.6kW than 4.5kW motors. Two nice safety improvements over the original Yozma IN10 include the magnetic kill switch and brake lights on the IN11.

If we are keeping it real here, there are dozens of similar-sized and spec’d mini-e-motos out there, often at a much lower cost than the Yozma IN11. But I’d argue that as the biggest and most trusted of these brands, Yozma is a safer bet.

Also, the IN11 is just a lot more solid than the random Amazon/Alibaba electric pit bike. Putting the IN11 together is quicker and easier than any other emoto I’ve built, and it just feels a lot more solid.

That feeling extends to the safety features. The brakes are more dialed in. The turning feels a lot tighter, and the overall ride is quieter and lighter. I believe, and my limited testing bears this out, that spec for spec, I got a lot more range on the IN11 than I got on other bikes with similar battery and motor specs. That 200nm of torque feels like it belongs on a much more expensive e-moto.

The smart wheelie mode is a nice trick (15, 25, or 40 degrees wheelie settings) and something we’ve only seen on Anylands for this price point so far. It is less of a standout feature on the IN11, and we expect to see this on just about every new pit bike coming out over the next few years. In fact, we’ve got another one in the review queue now.

That said, the price, which is currently fluctuating between $1299 and $1499 (don’t forget your $100 off 9TO5TOYS100 code), Yozma is going to be on the more expensive side of the 4.5kW emotos out there and some of the less established and more sketchy newcomers are bringing an intense value competition to the place where Yozma once dominated by itself.

#4837. RFK Jr.’s Revised Vaccine Schedule May Cause 83% Surge in Hepatitis B Infections

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers.

Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.

A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommends individual-based clinical decision making.

After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary.

Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates.

“Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” said Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

“The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse said. “There has been no new data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.”

Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team.

A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario.

With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination.

The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing.

Another study published in JAMA Pediatrics in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted.

However, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendation shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Under the new approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old.

The change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance.

However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines.

Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver.

Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults.

Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B.

“We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse said.

Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer.

“The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse said.

Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection.

“Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse said.

“The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.”

In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy.

The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates.

The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data.

Tse said the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional.

“Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse said.

“Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.”

While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections.

Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series.

You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection.

An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination plan for your baby.

“I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse said.

“There have been no new studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse said.

#4836. The 6 Pieces of Gear That Keep Bear Grylls Adventure-Ready

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

The journeyman shares what keeps him fit and fitted when he’s on the move.

#4834. Your Cat's Brain Chemistry Is Closely Linked to Yours

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

It is easy to think that your cat doesn’t really give a damn about you. As long as they get their food, you might assume, you are of secondary importance at best. And your happiness or stress is not something cats have the remotest interest in.

As it turns out, all of this is false. As a new study shows, there is a close chemical link between the mood, stress level and various hormonal markers of cat owners and their pets. Cats may try hard to appear nonchalant, but they are extremely well attuned to the mood and happiness of their owners. And vice versa: The emotional and hormonal state of owners is influenced, often without noticing, by the emotional and hormonal state of their cats.

The study was conducted on 19 cat owners and their 29 cats and lasted for a full month. The oxytocin and cortisol content of the cats’ and the owners’ urine was monitored, as well as the self-report of the owners about their mood. And the major finding is that there is a positive correlation between the oxytocin content of the cats’ and their owners’ urine.

Oxytocin is often (somewhat misleadingly) labelled as the ‘love hormone' as its presence is indicative of wellbeing, happiness, and social bond. Cortisol, by contrast, is indicative of stress. The key result is that the oxytocin content of the cats’ and the owners’ urine fluctuated together—and this effect was stronger if the physical proximity between the cat and the owner was closer. And the cats’ hormonal levels also correlated with the self-report of the owners: When the cats had high oxytocin and low cortisol, the owners tended to describe themselves as happy and relaxed, whereas when the cats had low oxytocin and high cortisol, the owners were more likely to experience stress or gloominess.

One major question about this study—one that the authors did not aim to address—is about who influences whom. Is it that the cat’s happiness makes us happy? Or is it the other way round, and the cat feels whether we are stressed? Or maybe both? These questions will, no doubt, be addressed in future research.

But the lesson is clear: Cats are not as antisocial as they seem. We have more and more findings about just how attuned cats can be to the various psychological states of their owners. They may pretend that they don’t care, but by all accounts, they do. And as these new findings show, physical proximity can make this effect even stronger.
